guide.title: Simsbury, Connecticut: Copper Coins, Safety Fuses, and a Hilltop Tower
guide.intro: Simsbury was settled as "the Windsor plantation at Massacoe" and incorporated as a town in 1670, one of Connecticut's oldest. In March 1676, during King Philip's War, the town was pillaged and burned to the ground; residents sheltered in Windsor before returning to rebuild in the spring of 1677. The name's origin is uncertain — it may come from the English town of Symondsbury, or from early settler Simon Wolcott, known familiarly as "Sim." Simsbury claims a string of industrial firsts: the nation's earliest steel-making venture in 1728, the Colonies' first copper coins, minted in 1737 by Dr. Samuel Higley with ore from his Copper Hill Mine, and America's first safety fuses for blasting in 1836, a business that evolved into an aerospace and defense company still headquartered nearby. Gifford Pinchot, first chief of the U.S. Forest Service and founder of the Yale School of Forestry, was born here in 1865.

sections.heading: Massacoe to the Learned Blacksmith's neighbor
sections.body: Simsbury was settled as 'the Windsor plantation at Massacoe' and incorporated in 1670, one of Connecticut's oldest towns. In March 1676, during King Philip's War, it was pillaged and burned to the ground; residents sheltered in Windsor and returned to rebuild in spring 1677. The town's name is of uncertain origin — the English town of Symondsbury, or early settler Simon Wolcott, known familiarly as 'Sim,' are the two candidates. Simsbury strung together a remarkable run of industrial firsts: the nation's earliest steel-making venture in 1728, the Colonies' first copper coins in 1737 (minted by Dr. Samuel Higley from his own Copper Hill Mine ore), the first carpet factory in 1825, and America's first safety fuses for blasting in 1836, a business that grew into an aerospace and defense company still headquartered nearby. Gifford Pinchot, first chief of the U.S. Forest Service and founder of the Yale School of Forestry, was born in Simsbury in 1865; under his leadership, federal forest holdings grew from 56 million acres in 1905 to 172 million acres across 150 national forests by 1910.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Simsbury is a Farmington Valley town in northern Hartford County, reached by car northwest of Hartford. There is no passenger rail station in Simsbury; the nearest CTrail Hartford Line and Amtrak service is at Hartford Union Station or Windsor.

sections.heading: A tower, a flower bridge, and the state's biggest tree
sections.body: Heublein Tower, a 165-foot structure built in 1914 as Gilbert Heublein's summer home, stands 1,000 feet above the Farmington River Valley in Talcott Mountain State Park, reached by the moderate 2.5-mile Tower Trail; Republican leaders reportedly urged Eisenhower to run for president at a gathering here in the early 1950s. The Old Drake Hill Flower Bridge, an 1892 span restored as a pedestrian crossing in 1995, is decorated with more than 60 volunteer-tended flower boxes over the Farmington River. Also on the Farmington River is the Pinchot Sycamore — the largest known tree in Connecticut, dedicated to native son Gifford Pinchot. Millwright's Restaurant and Present Company, in the Tariffville village, anchor the dining scene, with Tulmeadow Farm Store for ice cream; The Simsbury Inn and the Simsbury 1820 House are the town's two lodging options.

faq.question: How do I get to Simsbury?
faq.answer: Simsbury is reached by car, northwest of Hartford in the Farmington Valley. There is no passenger rail station in town; the nearest CTrail Hartford Line and Amtrak service is at Hartford Union Station or Windsor.

faq.question: What is Heublein Tower?
faq.answer: A 165-foot tower built in 1914 as Gilbert Heublein's summer home atop Talcott Mountain, 1,000 feet above the Farmington River Valley with views spanning roughly 1,200 square miles. The 2.5-mile Tower Trail leads to it; the tower is open Friday-Monday, May through early November.

faq.question: What industrial firsts happened in Simsbury?
faq.answer: The nation's earliest steel-making venture in 1728, the Colonies' first copper coins in 1737, the first carpet factory in 1825, and America's first safety fuses for blasting in 1836 — a business that grew into an aerospace and defense company still headquartered nearby.

faq.question: Who was Gifford Pinchot?
faq.answer: The first chief of the U.S. Forest Service and founder of the Yale School of Forestry, born in Simsbury in 1865. The Pinchot Sycamore, Connecticut's largest known tree, stands beside the Farmington River in his honor.

faq.question: Where can I eat and stay in Simsbury?
faq.answer: Millwright's Restaurant is the destination fine-dining room; Present Company serves seasonal menus in the Tariffville village; Tulmeadow Farm Store is the local ice cream stop. The Simsbury Inn and the Simsbury 1820 House are the town's two lodging options.

places.name: Talcott Mountain State Park / Heublein Tower
places.summary: The 165-foot Heublein Tower, built in 1914 as Gilbert Heublein's summer home, stands 1,000 feet above the Farmington River Valley with views spanning roughly 1,200 square miles; the moderate 2.5-mile Tower Trail leads to it. Republican leaders reportedly urged Eisenhower to run for president at a gathering here in the early 1950s. Tower open May 22-November 2, 2026, Friday-Monday 10 a.m.-4 p.m.; the park itself is open daily 8 a.m. to sunset.

places.name: Simsbury Historical Society / Phelps Tavern Museum
places.summary: A 2-plus-acre campus of more than a dozen historic buildings centered on the 1771 Phelps Tavern, listed on the National Register of Historic Places; the society was established in 1911 and the Phelps family donated the tavern, barn, and land in 1962. Ellsworth Visitor Center open Thursday-Saturday noon-4 p.m., with guided tours Saturdays at 1 and 2:30 p.m., April-November.

places.name: Old Drake Hill Flower Bridge
places.summary: An 1892 metal-truss road bridge spanning 183 feet over the Farmington River; after a replacement bridge opened in 1992 it was restored in 1995 as a pedestrian flower bridge, now decorated with 62 flower boxes and 32 hanging baskets planted and maintained by volunteers. Free and open to the public.

places.name: Pinchot Sycamore
places.address: Along the Farmington River, Simsbury, CT
places.summary: The largest known tree in Connecticut and one of the two or three largest American sycamores in the United States, growing beside the Farmington River and dedicated to Simsbury-born conservationist Gifford Pinchot. Freely accessible roadside site.

places.name: Millwright's Restaurant
places.summary: Destination fine-dining restaurant led by chef Tyler Anderson, with a dining room, enclosed bridge, and tavern seating plus Sunday brunch.

places.name: Tulmeadow Farm Store
places.address: 255 Farms Village Road, West Simsbury, CT 06092
places.summary: A local institution on farmland with original ownership dating to the 1700s, famous for homemade ice cream served from walk-up windows alongside farm-raised beef, produce, and local goods. Farm store open daily 9 a.m.-9 p.m.; ice cream windows daily noon-9 p.m.

places.name: Present Company
places.summary: Well-regarded chef-driven restaurant in Simsbury's Tariffville village, offering seasonal menus including a tasting-menu option.

places.name: The Simsbury Inn
places.summary: Full-service New England inn in the Farmington Valley with Twigs Lounge (fireplace and terrace dining), a ballroom for up to 200 guests, and multiple room types; markets itself as a home base for Talcott Mountain State Park and Heublein Tower.

places.name: Simsbury 1820 House
places.summary: Historic country inn in an 1820 house, offering suites and deluxe rooms with check-in amenities (wine and chocolates) and an on-site restaurant, Soma Grille; a 2024 Kayak Travel Awards winner.

links.note: Simsbury borders Avon to the south, linked by Route 10/US 202 (Simsbury Road) through the Farmington Valley.
Simsbury was settled as the Windsor plantation at Massacoe; its residents sheltered in Windsor after King Philip's War burned the town in 1676.
Granby was incorporated in 1786 from a section of Simsbury; the 4,400-acre McLean Game Refuge still spans both towns.
